summary_en:
### World Models & Predictive Dynamics

Today's papers reveal a striking convergence around **world-action models**—architectures that jointly learn perception, action-conditioned future prediction, and planning within shared backbones. The dominant design pattern couples latent world models with policy learning, whether through mixture-of-transformers video diffusion (Perceive-Predict-Plan), view-decoupled geometry states (GeoState), or JEPA-based latent ranking for VLA verification (VeriVLA). A key emerging insight is**reciprocity**: unified causal training shows world modeling and action modeling mutually reinforce each other, while VLA-Δ and "What Should Robot Policies Learn to Predict?" systematically probe which supervision targets—action, latent-action, or future-vision—yield the best dynamics representations. Test-time adaptation is also maturing: T2-z optimizes environment latents for unseen physical configurations, and Plans-Are-Not-Executions closes the planning-execution gap by adapting frozen planners to controller-specific characteristics rather than substituting executed trajectories.

### Robot Learning & Vision-Language-Action Models

The VLA landscape is shifting from pure action imitation toward**dynamics-aware learning targets**. Several works now supervise explicit physical state transitions (VLA-Δ) or temporal latent actions (TS-WAM) to guide action generation, enabling learning from action-free videos. EgoJEPA pushes cross-embodiment transfer further by decoupling human priors from robot-specific control via effect-aware latent actions learned from egocentric video. Verification is becoming a first-class citizen: VeriVLA demonstrates that test-time action-chunk ranking via latent world models improves manipulation success without pixel reconstruction. Meanwhile, MAIA anticipates contact-rich manipulation anomalies by predicting future visual and force consequences—moving beyond reactive monitoring. Together, these papers suggest the field is converging on a recipe where policies learn *what to predict* (state transitions, latent actions, future features) rather than merely *what to do*.

### Multimodal Reasoning & Agentic Systems

A notable trend is the **repurposing of video generators as general-purpose perception and reasoning engines**. Gen4P shows that pretrained video generators transfer to feed-forward 4D perception with continuous-time queries, while CoWorld Reasoner embeds a video world model as a visual imagination engine within an agentic harness featuring co-evolving tools and skills. Intern Lumina U2 extends this with a multi-codebook diffusion LLM supporting video and 3D inputs. On the agentic front, the Gemini 4 Argon Minecraft run demonstrates sustained coherent planning over thousands of steps, and the proactive video assistant benchmark introduces risk prediction and intervention timing—both offering plausible, if indirect, evidence for long-horizon memory and anticipatory dynamics in agentic systems. "Can Visual Generation Expand What Unified Multimodal Models Know?" probes whether generation training transfers new knowledge to text-only QA, with alignment strategies relevant to unified generation-understanding training.

### Efficient Video & World Model Architectures

Efficiency and memory are being tackled through**spatial and temporal abstraction**. Velox introduces a training-free frustum-slab attention router that selects region-level historical context, accelerating long-horizon video world-model rollouts while preserving visual memory. Memory-as-Weights takes a complementary approach, internalizing long-term streaming history into evolving LoRA weights via a recurrent HyperNetwork—a transferable mechanism for long-horizon video and world models. ReState identifies a noise-level temporal mismatch in few-step diffusion and corrects masked predictions toward background evidence, a training-free insight applicable to efficient video diffusion editing. Constrained multi-agent RL in imagination moves constrained policy updates into learned rollouts, reducing environment interactions—another sign that learned simulators are becoming the default substrate for both training and evaluation.

### Representation Learning & Physical Understanding

Several papers probe the**geometric and physical structure latent in learned representations**. Local Temporal Contrasts on human motion data induce a latent geometry with coherent structure, while "How Much Physics Can Vision Learn from Audio?" distills audio-derived damping structure into vision encoders, showing multi-frame visual dynamics recover material properties. FutureLift refines multimodal motion forecasts via bidirectional future graphs, offering a transferable relational dynamics representation. GRASE closes the loop between real and simulated geometry through agentic render-vs-capture feedback, directly relevant to world-model construction. Collectively, these works suggest that self-supervised objectives over temporal and multimodal signals are uncovering physically meaningful latent structure—a foundation for more sample-efficient and generalizable dynamics models.

2610.22363.title: Perceive, Predict, and Plan: a Unified World Action Model for Egocentric Dexterous Manipulation
2610.22363.abstract: arXiv:2610.22363v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: We introduce P$^{3}$-WAM, a unified world action model for egocentric dexterous manipulation that learns 3D perception, action-conditioned prediction, and goal-directed planning through three complementary modes: Perceive, which reconstructs articulated hand motion and camera trajectories from video; Predict, which generates visual futures under prescribed actions; and Plan, which jointly generates action trajectories and their anticipated visual consequences conditioned on an initial image, a language instruction, and an optional visual goal. Our model integrates a compact, structured 3D action representation into a pretrained video diffusion transformer through a mixture-of-transformers architecture with shared base weights, modality-specific adaptation, and bidirectional visual-action attention. Randomized modality visibility lets video and 3D actions serve as either conditioning context or prediction targets across the three modes. Experiments show that unified training improves all three capabilities over single-mode training, including gains in planning quality under a vision-language model evaluation. Through unified training, our model outperforms specialized baselines on 3D hand reconstruction and action-conditioned video prediction across four datasets, while producing goal-directed manipulation videos with stronger instruction adherence and action progression than video-generation baselines. Project Page: https://p3-wam.pages.dev/
2610.22363.COMMENT: Unified world-action model that jointly learns 3D perception, action-conditioned visual future prediction, and goal-directed planning via a mixture-of-transformers video diffusion backbone with shared weights.

2610.22343.title: GeoState: Learning View-Decoupled Geometry States for 3D World Modeling
2610.22343.abstract: arXiv:2610.22343v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Recent 3D world models increasingly use features from geometry foundation models (GFMs) as predictive world states, benefiting from their rich geometric priors. However, the view dependence of these features entangles scene dynamics with camera-induced variation, making the resulting state evolution harder to predict. We propose GeoState, a view-decoupled geometry representation for predictive 3D world modeling that separates scene-state evolution from camera-dependent observation. Specifically, a scene tokenizer aggregates multi-view GFM features into a view-decoupled scene state, which a geometry decoder queries using camera rays. An autoregressive world model then predicts future scene states, while camera motion is modeled separately. The predicted states can therefore be decoded under either predicted or externally specified cameras, while retaining a single context-derived scale throughout the rollout without per-frame scale alignment. Experiments show that GeoState outperforms prior 3D world models on Waymo, supports geometrically consistent cross-view querying, and generalizes zero-shot to KITTI and nuScenes. Project page: https://hongchang-liu.github.io/GeoState-project-page/
2610.22343.COMMENT: Introduces a view-decoupled geometry state representation for predictive 3D world models, separating scene dynamics from camera-induced variation to enable geometrically consistent cross-view rollouts.

2610.22364.title: T2-z: Test-Time Optimization of Environment Latents for Robotic World Models
2610.22364.abstract: arXiv:2610.22364v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Predicting how the world responds to an action requires more than what can be seen: robots must account for environmental factors that are neither directly observable nor explicitly specified, from physical properties such as friction and mass to human-defined environmental rules. We introduce T2-Z for test-time optimization of environment latents, which augments a robotic world model with a learnable environment latent to condition world predictions. This compact latent captures underlying environmental variation without supervision of what environmental factors exist or what values they take. During training, T2-Z alternates between two stages: a world-model optimization stage that fixes the latents and learns general action-conditioned dynamics across environments; and an environment-latent optimization stage that freezes the world model and optimizes the conditioning latents, allowing latent structure to emerge purely through world prediction. At test time, the world model remains frozen and a newly initialized environment latent is optimized from one or more test-time interactions, adapting the model to previously unseen environmental configurations. Across 7 simulated settings and 4 real-world robotic tasks, T2-Z reduces object prediction error metric from 15.20 to 7.00 and raises action success from 33.73% to 72.96%. Its emergent latents capture structured representations of individual and compounded factors across diverse visual scenes. Ablations further show that T2-Z can efficiently infer environment latents from as little as a single test-time interaction trajectory.
2610.22364.COMMENT: Introduces test-time optimization of unsupervised environment latents that condition a robotic world model, enabling adaptation to unseen physical configurations and improving action-conditioned prediction.

2610.21686.title: MAIA: Anticipating Interaction Anomalies in Contact-Rich Manipulation via Multimodal World Models
2610.21686.abstract: arXiv:2610.21686v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Reliable contact-rich manipulation requires detecting execution deviations early enough for corrective action. Yet most monitoring methods are reactive, identifying anomalies only after they become observable. Anticipating such anomalies is challenging because visual observations only partially reveal physical interaction, while planned actions describe intended motion rather than their actual physical consequences. We address this problem with MAIA, a multimodal framework for anomaly anticipation. Its vision-action-force world model learns nominal interaction dynamics and predicts the visual and force responses of planned actions, while a lightweight anomaly head predicts impending interaction anomalies. To enable systematic evaluation, we introduce CRIA, a real-world multimodal dataset of 2,852 trajectories spanning 18 contact-rich manipulation tasks, with frame-level annotations of anomaly onset and evolution. Experiments on both seen and novel tasks show that MAIA achieves more accurate anomaly discrimination than representative baselines while providing earlier warnings, with bACC scores of 0.765 and 0.710 and median anticipation lead times of 28.0 and 25.1 steps, respectively. Moreover, using these predictions for anomaly-aware action selection improves end-to-end task success from 52.6% to 61.5% without retraining the underlying manipulation policy. These results highlight the value of modeling future physical consequences for proactive anomaly anticipation.
2610.21686.COMMENT: Builds a vision-action-force world model that predicts future visual and force consequences of planned actions to anticipate contact-rich manipulation anomalies earlier than reactive monitors.

2610.21922.title: TS-WAM: Temporal Latent Actions and World-Action Coupling for Vision-Language Robot Control
2610.21922.abstract: arXiv:2610.21922v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Many vision-language-action policies rely on action-labeled robot demonstrations and lack an explicit mechanism for predicting future visual states. These limitations hinder learning from action-free videos and can encourage overfitting to demonstration conditions, weakening generalization and robustness. We present TS-WAM, a lightweight Teacher-Student World-Action Model that addresses these challenges through self-supervised temporal learning and explicit future prediction. Its vlm-jepa framework learns from heterogeneous data, including robot demonstrations and action-free human videos, using an EMA target branch without requiring a separately trained external teacher. By coupling vlm-jepa with delta-lwm, TS-WAM learns to predict latent actions from the current observation and instruction and uses them to predict future visual features that guide action generation at inference. A unified end-to-end training architecture jointly optimizes temporal representation learning, visual dynamics, and robot control without a separate latent-action or world-model pretraining stage. The EMA target branch is removed at inference, keeping the deployed policy lightweight. Experiments on LIBERO, LIBERO-Plus, and SimplerEnv, together with real-world manipulation experiments on Franka Research 3 and RevoTron, demonstrate that TS-WAM achieves strong manipulation performance, generalization, and robustness.
2610.21922.COMMENT: Couples a self-supervised temporal latent-action model with a latent world model to predict future visual features that guide robot action generation, enabling learning from action-free videos.

2610.21985.title: VeriVLA: Adaptive Test-Time Verification for Flow-Based VLAs with Latent World Models
2610.21985.abstract: arXiv:2610.21985v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Flow-based Vision-Language-Action (VLA) policies are inherently stochastic: different noise seeds can produce action chunks of varying quality from the same observation. At test time, however, the policy typically commits to a single sample without an explicit estimate of its quality. In fine-grained manipulation, executing a suboptimal action can irreversibly disrupt task progress and lead to failure. To exploit policy stochasticity, we introduce a training-free two-axis trigger that uses two initial samples to measure within-chunk temporal variation and cross-sample variance, detecting the critical states. Once triggered, a JEPA-based latent world model ranks candidate action chunks by predicting action-conditioned future latent states and the corresponding changes in task progress. By operating in latent space, the verifier avoids pixel reconstruction and enables efficient and more accurate ranking. Across three real-world tasks, $\textit{i.e.,}$ pen insertion, pipetting, and apple placement), our method raises the average completion score from 50.8% to 65.5%, while adding 326 ms for sampling and verification per triggered decision on a single RTX 4090. Consistent gains are also observed in simulation, where the average success rate rises from 66.4% to 73.6% in the clean setting of RoboTwin 2.0, from 62.8% to 69.6% in its randomized setting, and from 96.9% to 97.6% on LIBERO.
2610.21985.COMMENT: Uses a JEPA-based latent world model to rank action chunks by predicting action-conditioned future latents and task-progress changes, improving VLA manipulation success without pixel reconstruction.

2610.22311.title: Velox: Spatial Memory Makes World Models Efficient
2610.22311.abstract: arXiv:2610.22311v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Video world models turn actions and camera motion into long visual rollouts, making video a natural interface for interactive simulation. Such interaction requires responsive generation, yet coherent rollouts must retain visual memory of what has already been generated. Chunked video diffusion models usually keep this context in growing KV caches, so later chunks become progressively slower. To address this bottleneck, we introduce Velox, a training-free attention router for region-level context selection using frustum slab correspondences from streaming geometry. Velox represents historical blocks as camera frustum slabs with depth intervals and obtains current-block depth through recency-priority multiwarp. For well-covered regions, frustum slab overlap softly modulates each layer's model-derived block importance. Uncovered regions retain the model-derived route without geometric bias. The fixed token-block granularity matches FlashAttention-style tiled execution and reduces the attention term that grows with rollout length. Frustum slab construction runs asynchronously with denoising on the same H200. At chunk 48, Velox accelerates attention by $4.36\times$ and denoising by $2.43\times$. On the full 158-case WBench navigation split, it remains within 0.15 API-free average points of dense LingBot-Fast-Cam. Please see our project page at https://velox-world.com/velox/ for more details.
2610.22311.COMMENT: Training-free frustum-slab attention router that selects region-level historical context to accelerate long-horizon interactive video world-model rollouts while preserving visual memory.

2610.20904.title: EgoJEPA: Beyond Retargeting for Dexterous Manipulation from Egocentric Videos
2610.20904.abstract: arXiv:2610.20904v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Egocentric human videos offer a scalable alternative to costly robot demonstra- tions, yet transferring their manipulation priors to robot control remains chal- lenging. The commonly adopted retargeting-based approaches convert human wrist and finger poses into embodiment-specific action commands through hand- crafted geometric mappings. However, such mappings require meticulous recal- ibration across different embodiments and risk propagating hand-tracking errors into downstream robot control pipelines. To this end, we propose EgoJEPA, a three-stage framework that learns embodiment-agnostic representations from ego- centric human videos without rule-based human-to-robot retargeting: 1) Human- action pre-training learns effect-aware latent actions through JEPA-style visual prediction conditioned on hand-motion differences; 2) Latent-action-based world modeling jointly predicts future visual dynamics and latent actions, which decou- ples human prior pre-training from robot-specific control parameterizations; 3) Embodiment-specific tuning adapts the pretrained model to diverse robots through lightweight action adapters. Experiments on five real-world manipulation tasks across three robot embodiments demonstrate the effectiveness and efficiency of EgoJEPA. It achieves a 74% average success rate under the out-of-domain evalu- ation, compared with 65% for the retargeting baseline, while reducing cumulative cross-embodiment wall-clock cost by 47.2%, from 743.2 to 392.7 hours.
2610.20904.COMMENT: Learns effect-aware latent actions and a latent-action world model from egocentric human video, decoupling human priors from robot-specific control for cross-embodiment manipulation.

2610.21095.title: Can World and Action Modeling Benefit Each Other under Unified Causal Training?
2610.21095.abstract: arXiv:2610.21095v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: World and action modeling are closely related, yet their reciprocal benefits under unified causal training remain unclear. We introduce OneWM, a simple framework for unified causal training that treats actions as both conditions for world prediction and targets for policy learning within a shared video-action architecture. Using this framework, we investigate whether learning forward dynamics conditioned on specified actions improves action learning, and whether learning to generate actions in turn improves action-conditioned world modeling. We use LIBERO, LIBERO-Plus, and RoboCasa365 as embodied testbeds to evaluate both policy learning and world modeling, complemented by real-world policy experiments. Learning the visual consequences of specified actions improves policy performance and generalization across changing scenes. In turn, action learning improves multi-view world-prediction fidelity under the same architecture. Together, these results answer both questions positively, supporting reciprocal benefits between world modeling and action generation under unified causal training.
2610.21095.COMMENT: Unified causal training framework showing reciprocal benefits between action-conditioned video world modeling and policy learning in a shared video-action architecture.

2610.22371.title: Gen4P: Video Generators are 4D Perceivers
2610.22371.abstract: arXiv:2610.22371v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: We introduce Gen4P, a unified framework for recovering 4D geometry and motion from monocular video. We show that a pretrained video generator can be repurposed into a feed-forward 4D perceiver without iterative denoising. Building on on-demand querying, Gen4P processes clean video latents in a single encoder pass and predicts the requested 4D attributes through a lightweight cross-attention decoder. The on-demand query formulation enables flexible spatial sampling, and our proposed continuous-time queries further provide temporal flexibility. To strengthen geometric knowledge, we propose a straightforward plug-in solution by incorporating a pretrained video-depth LoRA as a frozen geometry prior, improving overall performance without adding extra trainable parameters. Gen4P achieves state-of-the-art or competitive performance on tasks of 3D point tracking, video depth and camera pose estimation. Qualitative results on in-the-wild videos illustrate its capability of tracking complex motion while maintaining the delicate structure. Together, these results demonstrate the potential of video generative pretraining for unified 4D perception. See https://gen4p.github.io for more visual results.
2610.22371.COMMENT: Repurposes a pretrained video generator as a feed-forward 4D perceiver with continuous-time on-demand queries, showing video generative pretraining transfers to geometry and motion understanding.

2610.21910.title: CoWorld Reasoner: Agentic Multimodal Reasoning with the Evolving Video World Model-Driven Harness
2610.21910.abstract: arXiv:2610.21910v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: As Vision-Language Models (VLMs) advance, they are increasingly expected to perform spatiotemporal reasoning over motion, actions, and view changes beyond what the input images show. Video World Models (VWMs) provide a natural unified engine for visual imagination by generating task-relevant visual content as additional evidence. However, existing approaches typically invoke a VWM through fixed pipelines centered on a predefined form of visual imagination, such as novel-view synthesis. To support flexible visual imagination for diverse reasoning tasks, we introduce CoWorld Reasoner, an agentic framework that uses a VWM as a unified visual reasoning engine. Its Video World Model-Driven Harness exposes multiple visual operations through tools and uses skills to guide the VLM in deciding whether to imagine, selecting an operation, constructing a generation request, and interpreting the resulting visual evidence. We further introduce VLM-VWM Harness Co-Evolution, which jointly revises tools, skills, and execution code based on execution feedback while keeping both model weights fixed. Across seven benchmarks spanning spatial intelligence, temporal and causal reasoning, and perceptual reasoning, CoWorld Reasoner outperforms direct reasoning with the same VLM. The strongest variant improves on all seven benchmarks, including relative accuracy gains of 11.8% on MMSI and 13.0% on ERQA, and outperforms all five evolving baselines using the same backbone across five benchmarks.
2610.21910.COMMENT: Uses a video world model as a unified visual imagination engine within an agentic reasoning harness, with co-evolution of tools and skills for flexible spatiotemporal reasoning.

2610.22041.title: Plans Are Not Executions: Adapting Frozen World-Model Planners to Controller-Induced Execution Shift
2610.22041.abstract: arXiv:2610.22041v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: World-model planners evaluate candidate trajectories by predicting their future consequences, implicitly relying on the plan-to-motion relationship learned during training. At deployment, a different downstream controller may execute the same planned trajectory differently, creating a planning-execution gap between the frozen model's imagined future and actual execution. A natural remedy is to replace the planned trajectory with its predicted or observed execution. However, we find that better execution fidelity does not necessarily yield better decisions: directly substituting predicted execution trajectories yields only a 0.048 PDMS improvement across 10 unseen controller configurations, far smaller than the gain from our proposed adaptation. This suggests a semantic mismatch between a planned trajectory, which serves as a reference for downstream control, and an executed trajectory, which already describes the resulting post-controller motion.   We introduce ExecutionBridge, which infers controller-specific execution characteristics from planned-executed trajectory pairs and uses them to adapt the native ego latent rollout while keeping the original planned trajectory unchanged. The planner, world model, and reward head remain frozen. On NAVSIM, ExecutionBridge consistently improves planning across unseen controller configurations and multiple frozen world-model planners, with substantially larger gains in challenging driving scenes where execution mismatch more strongly affects candidate evaluation.
2610.22041.COMMENT: Shows that adapting a frozen world-model planner's latent rollout to controller-specific execution characteristics, rather than substituting executed trajectories, closes the planning-execution gap.

2610.21319.title: Constrained Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning in Imagination
2610.21319.abstract: arXiv:2610.21319v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Predicting cost in a multi-agent world model moves most constrained policy updates into imagination: the stronger model-free baseline needs $10$ to $20$ times CA-MAMBA's interactions on the median SMAC configuration, and CA-MAMBA earns $2.8$ to $12$ times the baselines' MAMuJoCo reward at equal budget. In controlled tests on one task per benchmark, pricing the model's cost advantages at parity more than halves a cost-blind learner's cost and meets a tight continuous-control limit the learned multiplier misses, suggesting the model's cost estimates are not the bottleneck.
2610.21319.COMMENT: Learns a multi-agent world model that predicts cost in imagination, moving constrained policy updates into learned rollouts and reducing environment interactions.

2610.22070.title: Memory as Weights: Internalizing Long-Term History for Streaming Videos
2610.22070.abstract: arXiv:2610.22070v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Streaming vision-language models (VLMs) must continuously integrate information from the past while remaining responsive to current observations and user queries. Existing memory mechanisms typically compress, retrieve, or cache historical observations and reintroduce them into the input context, forcing historical memory and current observations to compete for limited context. We propose MaLoW, a streaming memory framework that instead internalizes historical context into evolving lightweight parameter updates. MaLoW uses a recurrent HyperNetwork to incrementally consolidate incoming video observations into fixed-size LoRA weights, allowing historical information to be carried forward without revisiting the full video stream. In doing so, MaLoW represents history as weights, while keeping the current observation as input. To support training, we further construct MaLoW-Instruct, a large-scale streaming video dataset containing 381K question-answer pairs over 56K videos. We conduct extensive experiments to demonstrate that MaLoW achieves strong performance on OVO-Bench, StreamingBench, and StreamArena. On the backward split of OVO-Bench, MaLoW outperforms prior memory approaches by 3.9% to 11.8% across different video backbones while incurring only modest latency overhead. Beyond streaming video understanding, MaLoW also generalizes to vision-language-action models, improving the action success rate on Simpler WidowX by 9.3%.
2610.22070.COMMENT: Internalizes long-term streaming video history into evolving LoRA weights via a recurrent HyperNetwork, offering a transferable memory mechanism for long-horizon video/world models.

2610.22215.title: FutureLift: Lifting Trajectory Proposals into Bidirectional Future Graphs for Motion Forecasting
2610.22215.abstract: arXiv:2610.22215v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Accurate motion prediction is critical for safe autonomous driving, yet even strong forecasters leave residual errors in their multimodal proposals. Existing refiners compress complete proposals or update their segments sequentially, preventing the full proposed future from serving as explicit relational context for correction. We introduce FutureLift, a backbone-agnostic refiner that represents each multimodal proposal as a heterogeneous future graph, with spatially grounded temporal nodes connected to agent histories, map elements, alternative modes, and, for joint prediction, other agents future trajectories. Bidirectional temporal edges allow later evidence to revise earlier segments in a single pass, and the updated nodes predict residual coordinate and confidence corrections. Requiring only proposals, scores, and scene context, FutureLift provides a common refinement interface for structurally different forecasting backbones. On Argoverse2 and the Waymo Open Motion Dataset, it consistently improves frozen proposals and outperforms native and specialized refiners across marginal and joint forecasting. On the WOMD motion-prediction leaderboard, FutureLift ranks first in minADE (0.5049m) and minFDE (0.9942m) among the compared standard-input methods, without LiDAR or ensembling, while achieving a competitive 0.4874 Soft mAP.
2610.22215.COMMENT: Refines multimodal motion forecasts via bidirectional future graphs, offering a transferable relational dynamics representation for long-horizon trajectory prediction.

2610.21287.title: ReState: Noise-Level-Aware State Correction for Training-Free Object Removal in Few-Step Diffusion Models
2610.21287.abstract: arXiv:2610.21287v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Training-free object removal commonly redirects self-attention away from the target region, but on few-step distilled diffusion models this often leaves object-shaped residuals. We identify a temporal mismatch: a structured prediction forms inside the mask at the first forward, and the short trajectory offers few later chances to revise it, while attention rerouting acts mainly in later steps. Across four distilled backbones, magnitude-matched single-forward interventions show that background-directed state correction affects the final result more than attention rerouting. We therefore propose ReState, which corrects the masked clean prediction toward background evidence retrieved from the input using a noise-level-aware weight that vanishes at the final forward. ReState retains object-excluding attention as a complementary constraint and adds no denoiser evaluations. Across two paired benchmarks and two few-step backbones, ReState achieves the best masked PSNR, SSIM, and LPIPS among training-free methods, improving PSNR by 3.17 dB on average over the strongest baseline. On OBER-Test, it also outperforms the 50-step attention-forcing reference on all three metrics at 6.7x lower latency. The same configuration transfers to two additional distilled backbones without retuning. Project page: https://tdrlee.github.io/ReState
2610.21287.COMMENT: Identifies a noise-level temporal mismatch in few-step diffusion and corrects masked clean predictions toward background evidence, a training-free insight transferable to efficient video diffusion editing.

2610.22221.title: How Much Physics Can Vision Learn from Audio? Probing and Distilling Damping Structure
2610.22221.abstract: arXiv:2610.22221v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Physical understanding is crucial for decision making, yet vision models struggle to infer properties such as damping that govern how materials behave. Audio encodes such properties directly, because an object's acoustic response to impact reveals its damping through measurable decay. We probe frozen encoders for the quality factor $Q$, a dimensionless measure of how many oscillations an object completes before its ring dies away, and report how well each embedding orders impacts by $Q$ using the Spearman rank correlation $\rho$, for which $\rho=1$ is a perfect ordering and $\rho=0$ an unrelated one. Audio embeddings reach $\rho=0.73$ and retain most of that advantage on materials withheld from training, while a single video frame taken at the moment of impact, encoded by CLIP, supports only $\rho=0.28$. Having established where the signal lives, we ask how much of that gap vision can recover. We distill a frozen audio teacher into a frozen CLIP backbone through a trained projection head and find that this recovers a useful fraction of the audio advantage. Because pooled correlations on this task are dominated in practice by category identity, we also evaluate under a leave-one-material-out protocol in which the held-out material is withheld from the projection head as well as the probe. Distillation with a four-frame input improves the correlation there from 0.234 to 0.338 (+0.053 over the matched four-frame baseline, 14 of 17 materials), a gain that no category-level strategy can produce. Widening the visual input to four frames spanning the impact supplies half of that improvement at no acoustic cost, which indicates that part of what a single frame misses is visible dynamics.
2610.22221.COMMENT: Probes and distills audio-derived damping structure into vision encoders, showing multi-frame visual dynamics recover physical material properties relevant to learned dynamics representations.

2610.21915.title: What Should Robot Policies Learn to Predict? Rethinking Supervision Targets in Vision-Language-Action Learning
2610.21915.abstract: arXiv:2610.21915v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) policies are typically trained with action prediction as the primary supervision signal, since robots ultimately execute actions. Auxiliary objectives such as latent-action (LA) and future-vision (FV) prediction are often added to improve policy learning, yet they compete with action prediction for the same training budget. We ask whether, under a fixed budget, allocating a substantial share of training samples to such objectives, rather than to further action prediction, can improve policy learning. We build a unified VLA framework that couples a two-stream multimodal diffusion transformer (MMDiT) with a sample-level router, which assigns each training sample to either action prediction or an auxiliary objective and thus makes supervision allocation explicit. Within this framework, we instantiate three LA targets based on LAPA and its DINO-feature variants, and three FV targets based on DINOv3, V-JEPA 2, and Wan2.2 representations. Across LIBERO, CALVIN, and four real-robot tasks, suitable LA and FV supervision outperforms action-only training under the same budget, even when action prediction receives no more than half of the training samples. FV generally outperforms LA, although the strongest LA target remains competitive on CALVIN. Diagnostic analyses suggest that DINO-based LA targets emphasize relative motion, whereas FV targets emphasize absolute position and task identity. We therefore argue that what robot policies learn to predict, and how training is allocated among these targets, should be treated as explicit design choices rather than defaulting to action-dominant training.
2610.21915.COMMENT: Systematically studies supervision-target allocation between action prediction, latent-action, and future-vision objectives in VLA learning, yielding insights on what dynamics policies should predict.

2610.21498.title: GRASE: Geometry-native Real-to-sim Agentic Scene Modeling from Video
2610.21498.abstract: arXiv:2610.21498v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Real-to-sim conversion aims to turn a captured video of a real environment into an editable 3D scene while preserving the geometry and layout of what was observed. Existing methods often follow a one-pass, loosely coupled paradigm: each stage receives only limited feedback from previous stages, allowing errors to propagate without reliable correction and leaving the final scene inconsistent. We present GRASE, an agentic framework that closes this loop by treating the captured multi-view video observations as a standing reference throughout scene modeling. Instead of committing to intermediate estimates, GRASE revises its current hypothesis whenever rendered evidence disagrees with the capture, overcoming the fixed intermediate assumptions of conventional pipelines. Specifically, GRASE first fits the architectural shell and its openings from depth and multi-view cues. An agent then places generated assets in a shared coordinate frame while checking their spatial relationships. Finally, each asset's geometry and placement are refined iteratively to improve agreement across the observed views. By coupling these steps through feedback, GRASE localizes structural discrepancies and revises only the responsible components, while preserving cross-view consistency. The resulting 3D scenes are faithful to the input, consistent across views, and suitable for simulations. In our experiments, GRASE substantially outperforms other state-of-the-art methods, including a direct real-to-sim conversion using GPT6-Astra.
2610.21498.COMMENT: Agentic real-to-sim pipeline that iteratively refines 3D scene geometry from video via render-vs-capture feedback, offering a closed-loop scene-modeling insight relevant to world-model construction.

2610.21306.title: VLA-$\Delta$: Learning Physical State Transition for Vision-Language-Action Models
2610.21306.abstract: arXiv:2610.21306v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) models transfer semantic knowledge acquired through vision-language pretraining to robot control, achieving strong performance across various benchmarks. However, most VLAs directly map observations to demonstrated actions without explicit supervision of intermediate physical state changes, making them prone to overfitting observation-action correspondences. Some methods introduce intermediate reasoning or future-state prediction in language, visual, or latent spaces to guide action generation, but do not explicitly supervise the physical state transition itself. We therefore propose VLA-$\Delta$, a general framework that uses physical changes between current and future states as explicit learning targets. To support this objective, we construct a large-scale pretraining dataset and derive physical state-transition annotations covering task-relevant semantics and visual motion changes, providing more direct supervision for continuous action generation. During inference, the model generates actions directly from current observations without additional inference overhead. VLA-$\Delta$ achieves performance competitive with the state of the art on LIBERO and RoboTwin, and outperforms $\pi_{0.5}$ in real-robot experiments. Our code is available at https://github.com/ZJU-OmniAI/VLA-Delta
2610.21306.COMMENT: Supervises explicit physical state transitions between current and future states to improve VLA action generation, providing a dynamics-aware learning target relevant to world modeling.

2610.21459.title: Can Visual Generation Expand What Unified Multimodal Models Know?
2610.21459.abstract: arXiv:2610.21459v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Unified multimodal models (UMMs) receive image-generation supervision that exposes them to visual information not fully documented in text. Can learning to generate images expand what pretrained models know? We introduce Knowledge Transfer Probing (KTP), a controlled protocol that supplies new knowledge through image-generation training and tests its accessibility through text-only question answering. Across seven knowledge categories and three UMMs, we observe direct but uneven transfer from visual supervision to language. Motivated by these observations, we successively introduce Textual Alignment and Interleaved Image--Text Alignment, which connect generation and answering through shared knowledge and interleaved responses, respectively. Guidance on selected entities can improve knowledge access on other entities without QA supervision, with additional gains from interleaved alignment. Further analysis shows that knowledge correctly reproduced in images is often more accessible through text, although substantial gaps remain between the two forms of access. These findings support visual generation as a source of knowledge beyond textual supervision, and motivate joint investigation of training data design and model architecture to make this knowledge more broadly accessible.
2610.21459.COMMENT: Probes whether image-generation training transfers new knowledge to text-only QA in unified multimodal models, offering a controlled protocol and alignment strategies relevant to unified generation-understanding training.

2610.21630.title: Local Temporal Contrasts on Human Motion Data Induce a Latent Geometry
2610.21630.abstract: arXiv:2610.21630v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Time series such as recordings of human motion data often encode structure across multiple temporal scales, and when a latent state determining this sequence evolves, this structure needs to survive in the representation space for downstream use. Yet the currently prevalent attention-based encoders paired with sequence-level pooling have made single-vector, pointwise comparison the default mode of inference, discarding the trajectory a sequence traces through the representation space. We propose recovering this geometric structure directly, without relying on forecasting-based objectives, by training an encoder model (SemTAC) with a temporal-neighborhood contrastive loss: representations that satisfy local consistency everywhere must give rise to a coherent global structure, letting inference happen at temporal scales beyond those seen during training. We evaluate SemTAC against four baselines on a five-step motion sequence discrimination task: the same architecture trained with a classification or a standard contrastive objective, and two established self-supervised time-series methods, TS-TCC and TS2Vec. At the full sequence length all five are broadly competitive, but on incomplete, truncated sequences SemTAC holds a large advantage: a median F1 of 0.77 one step before the sequence completes, against 0.27-0.70 for the four baselines. A hyperparameter-matched ablation attributes this effect specifically to the temporal-contrastive objective. SemTAC's representation trajectories are also the only ones among these five to exhibit interpretable geometric structures, exceeding a no-structure chance baseline on a displacement-smoothness metric which we introduce. This is evidence that its objective, not classification accuracy alone, produces genuinely temporally-ordered trajectories.
2610.21630.COMMENT: Temporal-neighborhood contrastive objective yields latent representation trajectories with coherent geometric structure, a potentially transferable representation insight for learned dynamics.

2610.20818.title: Intern Lumina U2: A Multi-Codebook Diffusion Large Language Model for Omni-Visual Understanding and Image Generation
2610.20818.abstract: arXiv:2610.20818v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Unified multimodal generation covers discrete, continuous, and hybrid paradigms. Discrete approaches with single-codebook visual tokenizers align naturally with text modeling but have limited representational capacity. Continuous and hybrid approaches retain richer visual representations, but they model text and images in heterogeneous spaces with different training objectives, potentially introducing optimization conflicts between modalities with misaligned representation spaces. These choices expose a central question: how to efficiently model high-capacity visual representations alongside textual content in a shared optimization space within a single backbone. We present Intern Lumina U2, to our knowledge the first diffusion language model to represent multi-codebook visual tokens in a fully discrete space. Each visual position is represented by a group of codes from complementary codebooks, increasing its representational capacity while preserving compatibility with discrete text modeling. At the input, the embeddings are concatenated at each position; at the output, a lightweight multi-codebook autoregressive head predicts the codes within each position sequentially, while the diffusion backbone processes all positions in parallel. Built on the unified 4D representation of AToken, Intern Lumina U2 supports image, video, and 3D inputs within a single backbone and achieves leading performance among unified models in visual understanding, image generation, and image editing. We further build a full-stack training, inference, and evaluation system on both Ascend and NVIDIA platforms to verify the cross-platform effectiveness of our model. We also improve the inference efficiency through a stability-aware sampling strategy, which combines confidence-plateau-guided unmasking approach with drift-triggered cache refreshing mechanisms, accelerating image generation by 4.45x.
2610.20818.COMMENT: Multi-codebook discrete diffusion language model supporting video and 3D inputs, with a stability-aware sampling strategy that could transfer to video generation efficiency.

2610.22319.title: A team of Gemini 4 Argon agents beats Minecraft
2610.22319.abstract: arXiv:2610.22319v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: We placed four Gemini 4 Argon agents in a sandboxed Minecraft survival world and gave them one goal: defeat the Ender Dragon. Each agent controlled a player via an open-source library called Mineflayer and coordinated with its teammates through in-game chat and shared memory. No one assigned roles or wrote game logic. The agents planned, wrote, and debugged every program themselves. Researchers could watch the run on a live dashboard and pause or stop it at any time, but they had no cause to intervene. Starting from a randomly generated world on Easy difficulty, the team wrote 2,783 programs and defeated the dragon in 27 hours and 14 minutes, dying 605 times along the way. To our knowledge, this is the first end-to-end autonomous completion of Minecraft by AI agents, achieved using only the standard Mineflayer library without pre-scouted seeds or other game-specific tools written by humans. Winning required the agents to keep a coherent plan across thousands of dependent steps for more than a day. Complex real-world software engineering and enterprise tasks demand the same long-horizon coding and multi-agent coordination. We describe the setup, how the run unfolded, the team's strategies (dividing the work, sharing what they learned, recovering each other's items), and the limits of the result.
2610.22319.COMMENT: Long-horizon multi-agent Minecraft run demonstrates sustained coherent planning over thousands of steps, offering weak but plausible insight into long-horizon dynamics and memory for world-model agents.

2610.21568.title: From Perception to Prediction and Intervention: Benchmarking Proactive Video Assistants in Real-Life Scenarios
2610.21568.abstract: arXiv:2610.21568v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Recent multimodal large language models have advanced video understanding, but existing benchmarks mainly evaluate whether models can interpret observed visual content. In real-world scenarios, assistants must additionally anticipate what assistance is needed and decide when to provide it. To address this gap, we introduce \textsc{P$^3$IBench}, a benchmark for proactive video understanding in real-life streaming scenarios. It evaluates three complementary capabilities: daily perception, risk prediction and intervention. We benchmark 12 representative open-source and proprietary video-language models, including streaming and adapted non-streaming systems. Our evaluation shows that current models struggle to make well-calibrated response decisions. Finally, we construct additional proactive training data and train \textsc{P$^3$I-Assistant-4B}, achieving improvements on several tasks, though gains remain uneven across capabilities. Together, these findings show that effective proactive assistance requires not only visual understanding, but also precise response timing and appropriate restraint.
2610.21568.COMMENT: Benchmark for proactive video understanding with risk prediction and intervention timing, offering limited but plausible insight into anticipatory dynamics modeling for assistants.
